passage:
[1] The summer I turned fifteen, my parents sent me to stay with my uncle Teodor, who ran a sign shop out of a garage in Marlow Falls. I had pictured computers and vinyl cutters. What I found instead was a long wooden bench a radio tuned to baseball, and rows of brushes standing in coffee cans like bouquets.

[2] Teodor painted every letter by hand, and at first I could not see why anyone paid him to. His customers could have bought printed banners for half the price: the bakery on Main Street, a family of beekeepers, a dentist who wanted his name in gold leaf. On my first morning I noticed that the jars of paint on the shelf above his bench was labeled in his own careful capitals, as if even his supplies deserved good lettering.

[3] He started me on the alphabet, I painted capital A's for three days. My first A's leaned like tired fence posts. Teodor would choose the least terrible in each row and circle it with a grease pencil. For two days I could not tell his circled letters from the rest. In other words, I began to see what he was choosing: the letters whose two strokes met cleanly at the peak and stood evenly on the line. A letter, he told me, stands the way a building does: if their base is crooked, nothing above it will look straight.

[4] By August, Teodor trusted me to repaint the bakery's front window, where the old gold letters had faded in the sun until they were barely visible and could hardly be seen. I traced their faint outlines onto paper before scraping the glass clean. Then I worked so slowly that the baker came out twice to ask whether I was still alive.

[5] By the end of the summer, I had lettered three customers' signs on my own: a truck door for the beekeepers, a price board for the hardware store, and a brass plaque for the dentist. Not one of them is perfect. Now, whenever I pass a hand-painted sign, I look first at the bottom of the letters. Checking, the way Teodor taught me, whether they stand evenly on the line. Usually I can tell which painters had someone circling the good ones.
prompt: In paragraph 4, in the sentence "By August, Teodor trusted me to repaint the bakery's front window, where the old gold letters had faded in the sun until they were barely visible and could hardly be seen," which choice is the most concise without losing meaning the paragraph needs in place of "had faded in the sun until they were barely visible and could hardly be seen"?
choices: had faded in the sun until they were barely visible
had faded in the sun until they were invisible
had faded and dimmed in the sun until they were barely visible
correct_answer: had faded in the sun until they were barely visible
explanation: "Barely visible" and "could hardly be seen" say the same thing, so the second is redundant, and "faded and dimmed" repeats itself the same way. "Until they were invisible" is shorter but changes the meaning: the next sentence says the narrator traced the letters' faint outlines, which could not be done if they could not be seen at all. "Until they were barely visible" keeps the meaning once.

passage:
[1] An octopus resting on a reef can disappear in under a second. One moment it is a pale, smooth lump on the sand; the next it has taken on the mottled brown of the rock beside it, along with the rock's bumps and ridges. Few animals can alter both their color and their texture, and none can match the octopus for speed.

[2] The color comes from thousands of tiny organs called chromatophores. Each one a stretchy sac of red, yellow, brown, or black pigment ringed by muscle. When the muscles contract they pull the sac open, spreading the pigment across a wider patch of skin, and the sac shrinks back to a speck as soon as they relax. Because these muscles are controlled directly by nerves, an octopus can send a new pattern rippling across it's whole body in less time than a blink takes.

[3] Octopuses are also among the most intelligent of all invertebrates. Iridophores reflect light in shimmering blues and greens, the way a soap bubble does. Leucophores, scatter every color equally, so they look white under white light and take on the tint of whatever light falls on them. With these layers working together, an octopus can match not only the shade of its surroundings but also their brightness.

[4] Color alone would not hide an octopus against a crusted rock. [A] These are small bands of muscle in the skin that, when they tighten, push the surface up into bumps, ridges, or branching spikes. [B] Within seconds, a smooth animal can grow a coat of points that resembles the coral around it. [C] Covered in such spikes, a diver can swim within arm's reach of an octopus and never see it. [D] When the threat passed, the muscles relax and the skin lies flat again.

[5] What puzzles biologists is that octopuses appear to be colorblind. Their eyes contain only one kind of light receptor, yet they match colors they should not be able to tell apart. One clue came in 2015, when researchers found light-sensitive proteins—the same kind used in eyes—in the skin of the California two-spot octopus. The skin itself, in other words, may detect light.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "One clue came in 2015, when researchers found light-sensitive proteins—the same kind used in eyes—in the skin of the California two-spot octopus," which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "proteins—the same kind used in eyes—in"?
choices: proteins—the same kind used in eyes, in
proteins, the same kind used in eyes—in
proteins—the same kind used in eyes in
explanation: "The same kind used in eyes" is a nonessential phrase that interrupts the sentence, and it must be set off by a matching pair of marks. The sentence is correct as written, with a dash on each side. A dash opening the phrase and a comma closing it, or a comma opening it and a dash closing it, mixes two kinds of punctuation for one interruption. Dropping the closing mark leaves the phrase open, so it runs into "in the skin" as though the proteins were "used in eyes in the skin."

passage:
[1] In the early 1800s, a French artillery captain wanted a way for soldiers to pass messages at night without striking a light that would reveal their position. His answer was "night writing," a code of raised dots punched into heavy paper and read with the fingertips. Each symbol stood for a sound rather than a letter, and a single symbol could use as many as twelve dots.

[2] The army never adopted the code. Soldiers found it slow to learn, and a message of a few words could take minutes to read. The captain then offered his invention to the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris. One of the first students to try it, in 1821, was a twelve-year-old named Louis Braille, who had lost his sight in an accident in his father's workshop.

[3] Braille saw at once that the code was clever but clumsy. A fingertip could not take in a twelve-dot symbol at one touch, so a reader had to slide back and forth over each one. Over the next three years, often working late at night, he cut the cell down to six dots; two columns of three. His father, a harness maker, had hoped the boy would one day take over the family workshop. The number of distinct patterns a six-dot cell can form are sixty-three, enough for the whole alphabet and common punctuation, and a fingertip can feel all six dots at once.

[4] Braille published his system in 1829, when he was twenty, and figured the school would totally love it. The school's staff, however, resisted it. Many sighted teachers preferred raised versions of printed letters, since reading them by eye, correcting them without special training, and to teach them required no new code. For a time the school even banned braille from its classrooms, but students went on passing it to one another in the dormitories.

[5] Braille died of tuberculosis in 1852 he was only forty-three. Two years later, France adopts his system as the official method for teaching blind students. Today a reader, who runs a finger along a line of braille, is still touching a soldier's idea, cut down to the size of a fingertip.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "Today a reader, who runs a finger along a line of braille, is still touching a soldier's idea, cut down to the size of a fingertip," which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "a reader, who runs a finger along a line of braille, is"?
choices: a reader who runs a finger along a line of braille is
a reader who runs a finger along a line of braille, is
a reader, who runs a finger along a line of braille is
correct_answer: a reader who runs a finger along a line of braille is
explanation: The clause "who runs a finger along a line of braille" tells which reader is meant; without it, "a reader" would be any reader at all, and the sentence would lose its point. An essential clause takes no commas. Setting it off with a pair of commas marks it as nonessential, which it is not. A single comma after "braille" separates the subject from its verb "is," and a single comma after "reader" opens an interruption that never closes.

passage:
[1] Ilse Brannock keeps a pencil behind each ear and a third in her shirt pocket, because the work she does produces more notes than one pencil can survive. For thirty-one years she has restored pipe organs, the towering wind instruments that fill the back walls of old churches and concert halls. Most of the organs she has repaired was built before anyone now living was born.

[2] An organ, Brannock likes to say, is less an instrument than a building that breathes. Air from a bellows, or in newer instruments from an electric blower, travels through a wooden chest and into rows of pipes, each one tuned to a single pitch. [A] A pipe the length of a pencil sings high and thin. [B] One the height of a two-story house produces a note so low that listeners feel it in their ribs before they hear it. [C] An organs voice depends on all of these pipes speaking at the moment the player expects them to. [D]

[3] The trouble is that organs age from the inside. The valves that let air into each pipe are hinged with leather, and leather dries, cracks, and eventually tears. Mice nest in the wind chests, damp warps the wood, a forgotten roof leak can ruin a century of craftsmanship in a single winter. When Brannock opens an instrument for the first time, she photographs every part before she touches anything.

[4] Brannock did not plan to inherit her father's trade. She trained as an accountant. She lasted four years in an office before she admitted that she missed the smell of hot glue and old pine. Her father, whom she still calls the best voicer she has ever met, had taught her one thing above all others, patience is not a virtue in this work but a tool, as necessary as any chisel.

[5] Last spring she finished a four-year restoration of an organ built in 1868 for a small church near the river. On the evening it was played again for the first time. The building filled with townspeople, and a few of the oldest had sung beside that organ as children. Brannock sat in the back pew with her pencils, listening for flaws.
prompt: In paragraph 4, in the sentence "Her father, whom she still calls the best voicer she has ever met, had taught her one thing above all others, patience is not a virtue in this work but a tool, as necessary as any chisel," which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "others, patience"?
explanation: The words after "others" spell out the "one thing" the father taught, so a colon, which introduces an explanation after a complete clause, is correct. As written, a comma alone joins two independent clauses, a comma splice. A semicolon followed by "and" doubles the joining device; a semicolon already does the work a conjunction would. Starting a new sentence with "That patience is not a virtue..." leaves a noun clause with no main verb, a fragment.

passage:
[1] Before a crossword reaches a newspaper, it begins as an empty square, drawn on graph paper or, more often now, on a computer screen. The person who fills it, is called a constructor, and the work is closer to engineering than most solvers suspect.

[2] A constructor starts with the theme entries, the long answers that stretch across the middle of the grid. Those entries are placed first. Nevertheless, every other square must eventually be built around them, both across and down. In a puzzle about weather, the theme entries might be phrases that each hide a kind of storm, and that hidden thread is what gives a puzzle their personality.

[3] The grid itself follows strict rules, every white square must belong to both an across answer and a down answer, and no answer may be shorter than three letters. The pattern of black squares must also look the same when the grid is turned upside down. Placing the black squares by hand, the symmetry is the first thing a constructor checks.

[4] Then comes the fill; the hundreds of shorter words that lock the theme entries together. Here software has changed the craft more than any other tool. A program can suggest thousands of words that fit a given pattern of letters, and it ranks them in order by how familiar and well-known they are likely to be. Yet the constructor still decides. A program will happily offer the name of an obscure Siberian river; a good constructor would rather rebuild an entire corner than make solvers guess at it.

[5] Once every square has been filled, the constructor turns to the clues, a separate art with its own rules. Some constructors fill their grids by hand, and others lean on software. Of the two methods, filling by hand is the slower, but its devotees say it produces grids with more character. Either way, the finished puzzle will be solved in perhaps twenty minutes by people who never think about the black squares at all.
prompt: In paragraph 1, in the sentence "The person who fills it, is called a constructor, and the work is closer to engineering than most solvers suspect," which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "person who fills it, is called"?
choices: person who fills it is called
person, who fills it, is called
person who fills it is called,
correct_answer: person who fills it is called
explanation: "Who fills it" is essential: it tells which person is meant, so it takes no commas, and no comma may come between the subject "The person who fills it" and its verb "is called." As written, a single comma separates the subject from its verb. Enclosing "who fills it" in commas wrongly marks an identifying clause as removable, leaving "The person is called a constructor." A comma after "called" separates the verb from its complement, "a constructor."

passage:
[1] For most of my life I have told people that I could not sing. I said it the way other people mention an allergy, as a plain fact about my body that no one could argue with. In second grade a music teacher asks me to "just mouth the words" during a holiday concert, and I took her advice for the next thirty years.

[2] Then last fall my neighbor Dolores, a longtime patron of the Eastfield Community Chorus, invited me to a rehearsal. I told her my usual line. She told me that the chorus had exactly one rule for joining, and it was showing up.

[3] The chorus, I soon learned, was not a gathering of polished voices. Our members came from nearly every neighborhood in Eastfield. The director a retired band teacher named Mr. Achterberg, never asked anyone to audition; instead, he listened to each newcomer speak for a moment and then pointed toward a section. He put me with the basses, in the back row, two rows behind Dolores and the other altos.

[4] During my first rehearsal I stood perfectly still and moved my lips, exactly as I had in second grade. The hardest part of those first weeks was not the notes but the silence between them, when I was sure everyone could hear that I was not singing. What changed it was the other basses' patience. They never once corrected me; they simply sang a little louder whenever I came in late, so that I could follow them.

[5] By December I was singing out loud, not well, but out loud, Mr. Achterberg noticed it before I did. He told Dolores and I that the basses finally sounded like a section. I still would not call myself a singer. But on concert night, standing in the back row, I sang the words—all of them, even the ones I was unsure of, instead of mouthing them.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "He told Dolores and I that the basses finally sounded like a section," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "Dolores and I"?
explanation: The pronoun is an object of "told," so it takes the objective form "me"; removing "Dolores and" shows it: "He told me." "I" is the subjective form, whether it comes after "Dolores" or before it. "Myself" is reflexive and is used only when the subject of the clause is the same person, but the subject here is "He."

passage_title: The Long Clock of the Bamboo
passage:
[1] Most flowering plants bloom on a calendar set by the seasons. A few bamboo species keep a different clock. One timber bamboo grown across East Asia flowers roughly once every 120 years, and when it does, nearly every plant in the world's scattered stands flower within a year or two of the others, whether it grows on a hillside in China or in a botanical garden on another continent.

[2] For centuries the pattern puzzled botanists, because the plants seem to have no way of signaling one another across oceans. Most researchers now think the timing is internal: each plant carries a kind of counter that began running when its parent stand last flowered. Bamboo spreads mainly through underground stems, so the plants in a forest are often clones of a single ancestor. They share a starting date. Nevertheless, they reach the end of the count together.

[3] What follows the flowering is as dramatic as the flowering itself. A stand produces an enormous crop of seed then it dies, often across hundreds of square miles at once. In northeastern India, one species flowers about every 48 years, and the flood of seed sets off a population explosion among rats. When the seed is gone, the rats turn to the farmers rice fields, and famine has followed several of these flowerings.

[4] Why would a plant wait so long and then spend everything at once? The most widely accepted explanation, first proposed by an ecologist in the 1970s, is that the strategy overwhelms the animals that eat seeds. If a bamboo released a little seed every year, mice, birds, and wild pigs could scarf down pretty much all of it. By flooding the ground with more seed than any population of seed-eaters can consume the plants ensure that some seeds survive to sprout.

[5] The long gap does its own work. Waiting decades kept the seed-eaters scarce between flowerings, so no large population is standing ready when the next crop arrives. A bamboo that flowered every few years would be feeding its enemies; one that waits a century is ambushing them.
prompt: In paragraph 2, which choice provides the most logical transition in place of "Nevertheless," in the sentence "Nevertheless, they reach the end of the count together"?
explanation: The plants are clones that "share a starting date," and reaching the end of the count together follows from that, so the relation is cause and effect: "As a result." "Nevertheless" signals that finishing together happens in spite of the shared start, which reverses the logic. "For example" would present finishing together as an instance of sharing a start date rather than a consequence of it, and "Instead" signals a replacement, as though the plants did something other than share a start.

passage:
[1] For about two centuries, London's river occasionally became its busiest street. In the coldest winters of what climate historians call the Little Ice Age, the Thames froze hard enough near London Bridge to hold crowds, and the city's residents—never ones to waste an opportunity, built a fair on top of it.

[2] The best-recorded of these fairs took place in the winter of 1683 to 1684, when the ice lasted about two months. Booths selling roast meat, gingerbread, and hot drinks lined a path down the middle of the river. Coaches drove across from bank to bank, people watched bull-baiting, raced horses, and played skittles. Printers hauled their presses onto the ice. They printed souvenir cards with each buyer's name. Even King Charles II bought one.

[3] The fairs were not a holiday for everyone. [A] The watermen who rowed passengers across the Thames earned nothing while the river was frozen. [B] Many of them made up the loss by charging a toll to anyone who wanted to step from the bank onto the ice. [C] Some even dragged his boat onto the ice to serve as booths. [D]

[4] The last frost fair opened in February 1814 and lasted only four days. Led across the ice below Blackfriars Bridge, crowds watched an elephant on one of those days. Then a thaw set in, and the river carried off whatever the stallholders had not cleared away in time.

[5] Winters did grow milder after the 1810s, but the main reason the fairs ended was that the river itself changed. The old London Bridge, which stood on nineteen narrow arches resting on wide stone platforms, were slowing the river so much that the water above it behaved almost like a pond. When the bridge was replaced in 1831 and the banks were later walled in by embankments, the Thames ran narrower, deeper, and faster. Moving water is much harder to freeze, and the river has not frozen solid in central London since.
prompt: In paragraph 2, in the sentence "Coaches drove across from bank to bank, people watched bull-baiting, raced horses, and played skittles," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "bank, people"?
explanation: "Coaches drove across from bank to bank" and "people watched bull-baiting, raced horses, and played skittles" are both independent clauses, so they must be separated as two sentences: "bank. People." The original joins them with only a comma, a comma splice, and removing the comma fuses them into a run-on. "Yet" is a legal joining word but signals a contrast, and the two clauses are parallel scenes from the same fair, not opposed ones.

passage:
[1] Most mapmakers today work from images taken by satellites or airplanes. Ines Varga cannot, because nothing she maps has ever seen the sky. For twenty-two years she has surveyed the caves beneath the limestone hills where she grew up, and the maps she produces is often the only proof that a passage exists at all.

[2] A survey moves through a cave in short, straight lines called shots. One person holds a target at the far end of each shot while another reads the distance, the compass bearing, and the slope from a handheld instrument. A third member of the team, the sketcher draws the walls, the floor, and how high the ceiling is as seen from each station. Varga has done every job, but she preferred sketching. "The numbers tell you where you are," she says. "The sketch tells you what it's like to be there."

[3] Cave passages rarely make the job easy. For instance, some are so low that the surveyors must crawl on their stomachs, pushing the instruments ahead of them. Varga once spent nine hours mapping a crawlway barely wider than her shoulders, it appears on the finished map as a thin line less than two inches long.

[4] Most new surveys begin with a phone call. A farmer feels cold air blowing out of a crack in a hillside, or a hiker squeezes through a gap in the rocks and finds that it keeps going. Varga drives out to look, and if the passage is real, she schedules a survey. She keeps every sketch she has ever drawn in a metal cabinet in her garage; the cabinets drawers are labeled by cave, and the oldest folders have gone soft as cloth.

[5] Varga's maps are slow to make, and they are meant to last. Most of the district's cave maps were drawn by her partners and her, and each one is accurate and correct to within a few inches. She knows that someone she will never meet may one day rely on one of them to find the way out.
prompt: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the sentence that ends "finds that it keeps going" in paragraph 4: "Caves like these form when rainwater, made slightly acidic by the soil, slowly dissolves limestone." Should the writer make this addition here?
choices: Yes, because it explains how the openings that the farmer and the hiker discover came to exist in the first place.
Yes, because it connects the hiker's discovery to the limestone hills that paragraph 1 says Varga grew up among.
No, because the paragraph traces how a new survey gets started, and how the rock dissolved plays no part in that.
No, because it contradicts paragraph 1, which places Varga's caves beneath hills of limestone rather than soil.
correct_answer: No, because the paragraph traces how a new survey gets started, and how the rock dissolved plays no part in that.
explanation: Paragraph 4 follows a sequence: a phone call, someone finding an opening, Varga driving out, a survey being scheduled, and then where her sketches are kept. A sentence on cave chemistry interrupts that sequence with information the essay never uses again. The sentence would indeed explain where the openings came from, and limestone does appear in paragraph 1, but neither of those is what this paragraph is doing, so neither is a reason to add it here. The sentence does not contradict paragraph 1; it says the limestone is dissolved by rainwater, not that the caves lie in soil.

passage:
[1] Libraries have existed in one form or another for thousands of years. Its driver, Lorna Petrakis, has steered it along the same ninety-mile loop through the hill farms of Bessemer County for eleven years, and she can name the reader behind nearly every mailbox on the way.

[2] The route was not always this long, in 2009 the bus stopped only at the county's four schools. Then parents began asking whether it could pause at the crossroads stores on the way back, and after that whether it could reach the farms beyond them. Now the schedule, which lists thirty-one stops and the hour of each, are taped inside every general store between Harlan Flats and the river.

[3] Lorna's readers are rarely who visitors expect. The most devoted is a retired dairy farmer named, Walt Okafor, who reads two westerns a week and returns each one with a pressed wildflower marking the last page. [A] Two teenage sisters ask her for graphic novels and, lately, for anything about veterinary school. [B] One woman, who has never once set foot in the main library, has worked her way through its entire shelf of Russian novels. [C] Lorna keeps a notebook of these requests and fills them the next time through. [D]

[4] Winter is harder. Having learned every hairpin on Kettle Ridge, the steep grades no longer worry Lorna, but ice is another matter. From December to March she takes the long way around the ridge, and the detour costs her three stops. She packs for those readers the way her grandmother packed a root cellar, everything they might want before spring goes on the bus in November. Walt, who is particular about the order he reads things in, gets his westerns numbered in pencil on the inside cover.

[5] The county board has twice debated retiring the bus to save on fuel and repairs. Both times, farmers who had never spoken at a public meeting drove into town and said things on its behalf. The bus is still running, and the wildflowers still come back, one pressed between the last pages of every western.
prompt: In paragraph 2, in the sentence "Now the schedule, which lists thirty-one stops and the hour of each, are taped inside every general store between Harlan Flats and the river," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "are taped"?
explanation: The subject is "the schedule," which is singular; the clause between the commas, with its plural "stops," does not change it. The sentence opens with "Now," so the verb must also be present tense: "is taped." "Are taped" and "have been taped" are plural verbs for a singular subject. "Was taped" agrees in number but puts the sentence in the past, contradicting "Now."

passage:
[1] The summer I turned sixteen, my grandmother decided that I would learn to drive on her truck, a 1994 pickup with a stick shift and a bench seat patched with duct tape. My parents cars were both automatics. Grandma Ines considered this a character flaw, and she said so at dinner more than once.

[2] Our first lesson took place in the empty lot behind the feed store. She named the clutch, the brake, and the gas, then she made me point to each one from left to right. When she took the wheel to demonstrate, she shifted smooth and quiet, as if the truck were an extension of her own feet. She taught me to listen to the engine, to watch the needle on the tachometer, and feeling the clutch through the sole of my shoe.

[3] I stalled the truck eleven times that afternoon, and each time the engine died with a shudder that I could feel in my teeth. Grandma Ines did not raise her voice. Similarly, she turned the key off, waited, and told me to try again. Even on the eleventh stall, my grandmother was totally chill about it, as though stalling were simply the price of the lesson.

[4] By the end of July we had graduated to the hill on Quarry Road. The hill that Grandma chose for my final test rose so steeply that I could see only sky through the windshield. The clutch on that truck—older than my mother, by Grandma's count, gave way without warning, and on a slope that meant rolling backward toward the stop sign. It had rained all morning, and the cab smelled the way it always did in wet weather, like the hay its first owner had hauled for his goats. On my third try I found the point where the clutch caught, eased onto the gas, and climbed.

[5] I drive an automatic now, like my parents. But when it rains I still reach for a clutch that is not there, and for a second I can smell hay.
prompt: In paragraph 4, in the sentence "By the end of July we had graduated to the hill on Quarry Road," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "we had graduated"?
explanation: The essay narrates a past summer, and "By the end of July" marks a point in that past before which the move happened, so the past perfect "we had graduated" is correct. "Have graduated" is present perfect, tied to the present rather than a past July; "graduate" shifts the narration into the present; and "will have graduated" projects the event into the future.

passage:
[1] Before photography, a family that wanted a likeness of someone it loved had few choices. An oil portrait could cost a year's wages, and even a miniature painted on ivory was beyond most households. The silhouette, a profile cut from black paper and mounted on a pale card cost a fraction of either.

[2] The method was simple. The sitter sat sideways beside a candle, and the shadow of his or her head fell on a sheet of paper pinned to the wall. The artist traced the outline and then reduced it with a hinged device called a pantograph. Skilled cutters skipped the tracing altogether. Working freehand with small scissors, a likeness could be finished in under a minute.

[3] Silhouettes were sold in many places. Cutters set up booths at county fairs, on seaside piers, and in the lobbies of spa hotels. A visitor could pay a few pennies, wait while the scissors moved, and walk away with a profile in an envelope.

[4] One of the busiest booths stood on the pier at Saltmarsh, where Marianne Vell and her sister cut portraits every summer from 1821 to 1839. The visitors who sat for she and her sister rarely knew that they were taking home only half of what was cut. Vell worked from folded paper. Doubling the black sheet so that a single pass of the scissors produced two identical profiles. One went home with the sitter, and the other was pasted into that summer's ledger beside the date and the sitter's name. A drawer of these ledgers, sorted by year, sits in the town museum today, and historians consult them to learn who visited the resort each summer.

[5] The fashion faded quickly after 1840, when the daguerreotype arrives and a sitter could have a likeness that showed every eyelash. Most silhouettes are unsigned, the cutters who made them were tradespeople rather than artists and did not expect their work to outlast the summer. Vell's ledgers are the exception, and they have outlasted nearly everything else on the pier.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "The fashion faded quickly after 1840, when the daguerreotype arrives and a sitter could have a likeness that showed every eyelash," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "arrives"?
explanation: The sentence describes a past event, "faded quickly after 1840," and the rest of the clause is in the past ("could have," "showed"), so the verb must be simple past: "arrived." "Arrives" shifts into the present, "has arrived" connects the event to the present, and "will arrive" puts an 1840 event in the future.
